summary:
MARGIN is a free browser game where you design and fly a crewed mission to Mars, then live with every kilo, watt and dollar you chose. Play it: https://snake799-fy.github.io/margin/

As Mission Director you go from concept to operation in seven phases built on NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels and NASA's four mission segments: choose a science objective, run a trade study (launch vehicle and launch window), pack the lander's cargo grid, pass a crew design review, land, run surface operations sol by sol, and read the mission report.

The six resources named in the challenge (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) stay on screen the whole game. Placement matters: a reactor next to the samples ruins them, a drill contaminates the sample tubes, and water next to the storm shelter halves the radiation dose. On Mars, a scout robot clears the fog, four fictional astronauts walk out in pairs with limited suit time, events grow out of your own design choices, and the ascent rocket leaves on a fixed sol.

The report explains why the mission succeeded or failed, so students learn real engineering trade-offs by living them, then redesign and fly again.
details: WHAT IT DOES MARGIN is a mission design and operations game for students aged 12 and up and for beginners. You are the Mission Director of a fictional crewed mission to Mars. You design the mission, then fly it, and every decision you made comes back later. The game runs free in any desktop browser, with nothing to install: https://snake799-fy.github.io/margin/ HOW IT WORKS (7 phases, concept to operation) 1. Concept (CML 1-2): choose the science question (ancient life, past climate or water ice) and the length of the surface stay. The objective decides which equipment is mandatory. 2. Trade study (CML 3): Heavy or Super-Heavy rocket (cargo vs. cost) and an on-time or late launch window (more cargo vs. higher dust storm risk). 3. Cargo (CML 4): pack a 7x5 lander grid. Every item costs mass, power and budget, and neighbours matter: heat (reactor next to samples or medicine), contamination (drill next to sample tubes) and radiation shielding (water next to the storm shelter). Ten combos reward good layouts. Budget and rocket capacity never fit everything. 4. Review: the crew reviews the design and points out risks before launch. 5. Landing. 6. Surface operations: each sol you drive a scout robot through fog to find hidden science targets and send astronauts out in pairs, limited by 8 hours of suit time, power, food, data, communications and a fixed ascent window. Events (dust storms, solar particle events, equipment failures, medical issues, relay loss) are triggered by your own design choices. 7. Mission report: scores for science, crew, engineering and efficiency, the main cause of success or failure, and "Redesign & fly again". HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE The challenge asks players to design, manage and simulate a complete mission. MARGIN covers mission objective and requirements, launch vehicle, launch window, spacecraft cargo and instruments, budget, mass, power, data, communications and mission lifetime, then simulates operations and explains the outcome. The six resources are always visible with green, yellow and red margins, so a trade-off is something you see and feel, not a table. BENEFITS AND IMPACT Students rarely experience a whole mission from concept to operation. MARGIN turns abstract trade-offs into consequences: the cheap solar panel that fails in a dust storm, the drill packed next to the samples, the science target left behind because the ascent rocket will not wait. Because the report shows why things happened, failure becomes a lesson and replaying becomes learning. Three difficulty levels, optional challenges and permanent upgrades keep it replayable in a classroom. CREATIVITY Spatial packing becomes systems engineering: where you put a part changes heat, contamination and radiation. A crewed mission adds human stakes (four fictional astronauts with health, skills and a voice), and the surface phase mixes mission control planning with real-time exploration. SCIENTIFIC VALIDITY The structure follows NASA's own design method (JPL Concept Maturity Levels, the four mission segments, Goddard Mission Design Lab disciplines). Events echo real Mars lessons: Spirit stuck in sand (2009), Curiosity's damaged wheels, Opportunity lost in a dust storm (2018). The crew and simulated Marswalks are inspired by NASA's CHAPEA analog missions. Game numbers are simplified for play, and the game says so. The map is hand-made and only inspired by a Jezero-style delta. TOOLS Godot 4 (GDScript) with Web export (HTML5/WebAssembly), hosted on GitHub Pages. Pixel art, 74 animations and chiptune audio were generated in code with Python scripts (AI-assisted, declared). Font: Press Start 2P (SIL OFL 1.1). TEAM AND PROCESS A team of two from Belo Horizonte, Brazil: Pedro (art direction and game design) and our student programmer, who wrote most of the game code. We cut multiplayer and multiple landing sites to deliver a complete, playable loop in 30 hours, playtested repeatedly and simplified every screen to one clear instruction. NEXT STEPS 2-4 player hot-seat where each player adopts a crew member, a CubeSat tutorial, real trajectories with NASA GMAT, and more landing sites. AI USE We used Claude (Anthropic) for code review and bug fixing, design documents and game data, pixel art and audio generated in code, and drafting text and translation. Every AI-generated image in our demo slides carries a visible "AI-generated" label, and the README and game/art/CREDITS.md list every AI-made asset, sound and script. Full declaration, prompts and work log: https://github.com/Snake799-fy/margin
